title: 128-bit computing
summary: 128-bit computing denotes architectures or designs where the fundamental word size or data path is 128 bits. While no general-purpose CPU operates on 128-bit integers or addresses, many processors use 128-bit vector registers for parallel SIMD operations on smaller data types. Specialized systems, compilers, and software libraries provide 128-bit integer and floating-point support, and the bit width appears in identifiers such as UUIDs, IPv6 addresses, and cryptographic keys. Marketing uses of the term for gaming consoles do not indicate native integer or addressing support.

mechanisms.title: SIMD vector operations
mechanisms.explanation: Modern CPUs employ 128-bit vector registers within SIMD instruction sets (e.g., SSE, AltiVec) to hold multiple smaller numbers—typically four 32-bit floats—and execute a single instruction across all values in parallel. The processor does not treat individual numbers as 128-bit values; the 128-bit width applies to the register, not the operand.

mechanisms.title: Software emulation and compiler support
mechanisms.explanation: Compilers such as GCC provide 128-bit integer types (__int128) for architectures where the native register size is smaller. These types enable 128-bit arithmetic through software emulation or multiple-precision routines, and the Rust language offers built-in i128 support compiled to LLVM. Availability depends on the compiler and platform.
